title: Where Your Flush Goes When There's No Sewer
summary: More than 1 in 5 US households aren't on a city sewer. Follow one flush through a septic system: the buried tank where solids sink and grease floats, the drain field, and the soil that does the real cleaning, plus what pumping and a failed system cost (US EPA).
tags: how does a septic system work
sources: More than one in five households in the US depend on individual septic (decentralized) systems or small community cluster systems; solids settle to the bottom as sludge, oil and grease float to the top as scum, the liquid wastewater (effluent) exits to the drainfield; the tank is a buried, water-tight container of concrete, fiberglass or polyethylene (US EPA, Learn About Septic Systems / How Septic Systems Work, 2026): https://www.epa.gov/septic/how-septic-systems-work

In the drainfield the wastewater percolates into the soil, which naturally removes harmful coliform bacteria, viruses and nutrients (US EPA, How Septic Systems Work): https://www.epa.gov/septic/how-septic-systems-work

Inspect at least every three years; tanks are typically pumped every three to five years; only flush human waste and toilet paper; keep out grease, wipes, diapers, coffee grounds and household chemicals (US EPA, How to Care for Your Septic System, 2026): https://www.epa.gov/septic/how-care-your-septic-system

Maintenance about $250 to $500 every three to five years; replacing a failed conventional system costs between $5,000 and $15,000 (alternative systems more); more than four billion gallons of wastewater are dispersed below the ground every day; a malfunctioning system can cause groundwater contamination that can spread disease (US EPA, Why Maintain Your Septic System, 2026): https://www.epa.gov/septic/why-maintain-your-septic-system
Indoor water use as much as 70 gallons per individual, per day (US EPA, How to Care for Your Septic System, 2026): https://www.epa.gov/septic/how-care-your-septic-system

Pump when the bottom of the scum layer is within 6 inches of the outlet or the top of the sludge layer is within 12 inches of the outlet (US EPA, SepticSmart homeowner guide, 2012): https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-06/documents/septicsmart_longhomeownerguide_english-print-ready.pdf

About one-third of new development is served by septic or other decentralized systems (US EPA Septic Systems Overview, last updated 2018, archived): https://19january2021snapshot.epa.gov/septic/septic-systems-overview_.html

scenes.narration: More than one in five American households don't flush into a city sewer at all.
In our sewer video, one drop rode the pipes to a treatment plant. For these homes, the treatment plant is under the lawn.
Every day, more than {4 billion|four billion} gallons of wastewater soak into the ground this way.
Today we follow one flush through a septic system: the tank, the field, the dirt that does the real cleaning, and why skipping one chore can cost thousands.
Part one: the tank.
The flush runs down one pipe into a buried, watertight tank made of concrete, fiberglass or plastic.
Inside, it sorts itself out. The heavy solids sink to the bottom and become sludge.
Grease and oil float to the top as scum. The liquid in the middle, called effluent, moves on.
That's why only toilet paper should go down. Wipes, grease and coffee grounds don't break down. They just pile up in here.
If you like seeing how everyday things really work, subscribe. There's a new system every other day.
Part two: the field.
Each new flush pushes older water out of the tank, into a drain field: a shallow, covered trench in the yard.
And here's the hidden plant: as the water soaks down, the soil itself removes bacteria, viruses and nutrients.
And the tank sees a lot of water. Indoor use can run as much as {70|seventy} gallons per person, per day, and all of it comes through here.
No big pipes, no plant down the road. A tank, a trench, and dirt.
Part three: the bill.
But the sludge never leaves on its own. The EPA says inspect every {3|three} years, and pump it out every {3|three} to {5|five}.
The signal: when the bottom of the scum gets within {6|six} inches of the outlet, or the top of the sludge within {12|twelve}.
A pumping costs about {$250|two hundred fifty} to {$500|five hundred dollars}.
Skip it, and solids can clog the field. Replacing a failed system runs {$5,000|five thousand} to {$15,000|fifteen thousand dollars}, or more.
And a failing system can leak sewage into the groundwater, where it can spread disease.
It isn't going away, either. The EPA has said about a third of new development is built on septic or systems like it.
So no sewer doesn't mean nowhere. Your flush sinks, floats or soaks into the dirt, and the dirt cleans it. As long as someone pumps the tank.
Pick your next system down here. A new one every other day.
